name: The Last Man
statement: If the last person alive destroyed every living thing before dying, harming no one, our sense that it is still wrong suggests nature has value in itself.
statementAccent: our sense that it is still wrong suggests nature has value in itself
meaning: The last man is a thought experiment in environmental ethics proposed by the philosopher Richard Routley, later known as Richard Sylvan, in his 1973 paper Is There a Need for a New, an Environmental, Ethic. Routley asks you to imagine the last human being, the sole survivor of the collapse of the rest of humanity, who, before he himself dies, sets about destroying every living thing he can, trees, plants, ecosystems, animals, out of nothing but whim or spite. Since every other human is already dead and no sentient being will ever be affected, no human interest is harmed by the destruction. Yet most people have a strong intuition that the last man's wanton destruction is wrong. Routley argues that this intuition cannot be explained by any human-centred, anthropocentric ethic, and that it points instead to the conclusion that nature and living things have intrinsic value, value in themselves independent of their usefulness to humans.
mechanism: The argument tests dominant Western ethics against the intuition. Routley frames the prevailing tradition around what he calls a freedom principle, roughly that one may do as one wishes provided one does not harm others or irreparably harm oneself. On that anthropocentric principle the last man does nothing wrong, because there are no other humans to harm and he is about to die anyway. But if we judge his destruction wrong, as most people do, then the anthropocentric principle is inadequate: it cannot account for a wrong that harms no human interest. The best explanation, Routley argues, is that the living things destroyed have value in themselves, so that destroying them is wrong regardless of any effect on humans. The thought experiment thus works by isolating a case where every human-centred reason to preserve nature has been removed, leaving intrinsic value as the only candidate to explain the persisting intuition, and so argues against anthropocentrism and for a genuinely environmental ethic.

examples.text: The last human, knowing no one else remains, sets about eliminating every plant and animal he can before he dies, harming no human interest at all.
A purely human-centred ethic permits the destruction, since no human is harmed, yet the strong intuition that it is wrong suggests such an ethic is incomplete.
Routley concludes that the wrongness is best explained by holding that living things have value in themselves, independent of any usefulness to humans.

variants.name: The last people
variants.text: Routley's related version imagining the last human community rather than a single individual, dismantling nature as it dies out, to the same anti-anthropocentric end.

variants.name: The character-defect reply
variants.text: The anthropocentrist response that the last man's act reflects a defect of character rather than a wrong done to nature, explaining the intuition without intrinsic value.

whyItMatters: The last man is a foundational thought experiment in the emergence of environmental ethics as a discipline in the 1970s, offering a direct argument against anthropocentrism and for the intrinsic value of nature. By constructing a case in which no human interest whatsoever is at stake, it isolates and challenges the assumption that only humans, or only sentient beings, can be the source of moral value, and it thereby opens conceptual space for regarding ecosystems, species, and living things as ends in themselves. The argument has been widely cited and debated in discussions of intrinsic value, deep ecology, and the moral standing of the non-human world, and it remains a standard starting point for asking whether ethics must expand beyond human concerns. Its enduring power lies in the sharpness with which it pits a common moral intuition against a purely human-centred framework.

working.text: imagine the last person alive, so that nothing he does to nature can affect any other human or sentient being.
notice the strong sense that his destroying nature for no reason is wrong, even though no human interest is harmed.
conclude that the persisting wrongness is best explained by nature having value in itself, so anthropocentric ethics is inadequate.

limits: The last man argument relies on the reader sharing the intuition that the destruction is wrong, and it is contested by anthropocentrists who explain that intuition without granting nature intrinsic value. Some argue the wrongness reflects a defect of the agent's character, a failure of virtue, rather than a wrong done to the living things; others appeal to hypothetical or possible future human observers, or simply deny that the intuition is decisive. Because the argument turns on a single vivid intuition rather than a demonstration, its force depends on how widely and firmly that intuition is held. The experiment therefore makes a strong case for reconsidering anthropocentrism rather than proving the intrinsic value of nature, and the debate it opened between anthropocentric and non-anthropocentric ethics remains unresolved.
misreadings: The scenario is not a prediction or a claim that such a last man is likely; it is a device to strip away every human interest so that the source of the intuition can be examined. It does not by itself prove nature has intrinsic value; it argues that intrinsic value is the best explanation of a wrong that anthropocentrism cannot account for, a conclusion anthropocentrists dispute. And the point is not that harming nature is wrong only when the last human does it, but that this extreme case exposes what an ordinary human-centred ethic leaves out, which is why the experiment is framed at the very end of humanity.
origin: Proposed by the philosopher Richard Routley, later Richard Sylvan, in his 1973 paper Is There a Need for a New, an Environmental, Ethic, presented at the World Congress of Philosophy, to argue against anthropocentrism and for the intrinsic value of nature.

sources.text: Environmental Ethics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Routley's 1973 last man argument, the destruction of nature harming no human interest, the challenge to anthropocentrism, and the intrinsic value of nature.
